title: Motion in Space
lead: An object whose position is $\kvecr(t)$ has velocity $\kvecrprime(t),$ acceleration $\kvecrdprime(t)$ and speed $\|\kvecrprime(t)\|.$ The acceleration splits into a part along the path and a part toward the inside of the turn. Gravity alone gives projectile motion, and Newton’s laws with the calculus of vector-valued functions give Kepler’s laws for the planets.
objectives: Describe the velocity and acceleration vectors of a particle moving in space.
Explain the tangential and normal components of acceleration.
State Kepler’s laws of planetary motion.
summary_html:
• If $\kvecr(t)$ represents the position of an object at time t, then $\kvecrprime(t)$ represents the velocity and $\kvecrdprime(t)$ represents the acceleration of the object at time t. The magnitude of the velocity vector is speed.
  • The acceleration vector always points toward the concave side of the curve defined by $\kvecr(t).$ The tangential and normal components of acceleration $a_{\boldsymbol{T}}$ and $a_{\boldsymbol{N}}$ are the projections of the acceleration vector onto the unit tangent and unit normal vectors to the curve.
  • Kepler’s three laws of planetary motion describe the motion of objects in orbit around the Sun. His third law can be modified to describe motion of objects in orbit around other celestial objects as well.
  • Newton was able to use his law of universal gravitation in conjunction with his second law of motion and calculus to prove Kepler’s three laws.

exercises.prompt: A particle moves in a path defined by the vector-valued function $\textbf{r}(t)=(t^{2}-3t)\;\textbf{i}+(2t-4)\;\textbf{j}+(t+2)\textbf{k},$ where t measures time in seconds and where distance is measured in feet. Find the velocity, acceleration, and speed as functions of time.

answer.solution: $\begin{array}{l}\textbf{v}(t)=\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)=(2t-3)\;\textbf{i}+2\textbf{j}+\textbf{k} \\ \textbf{a}(t)=\mathbf{v^{\prime}}(t)=2\textbf{i} \\ v(t)=\| \mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)\| =\sqrt{{(2t-3)}^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}}=\sqrt{4t^{2}-12t+14}\end{array}$ The units for velocity and speed are feet per second, and the units for acceleration are feet per second squared.

exercises.prompt: An object moves in a path defined by the vector-valued function $\textbf{r}(t)=4t\;\textbf{i}+t^{2}\textbf{j},$ where t measures time in seconds. a. Find $a_{\textbf{T}}$ and $a_{\textbf{N}}$ as functions of t. b. Find $a_{\textbf{T}}$ and $a_{\textbf{N}}$ at time $t=-3.$

answer.solution: a. $\begin{array}{lll}\text{v}(t) & = & r^{\prime}(t)=4\text{i}+2t\;\text{j} \\ \text{a}(t) & = & v^{\prime}(t)=2\text{j} \\ a_{\textbf{T}} & = & \frac{2t}{\sqrt{t^{2}+4}},a_{\textbf{N}}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{4+t^{2}}}\end{array}$ b. $a_{\textbf{T}}(-3)=-\frac{6\sqrt{13}}{13},a_{\textbf{N}}(-3)=\frac{2\sqrt{13}}{13}$<sup class="fn" data-note="c-cp15"></sup>

Let $\textbf{r}(t)=r\;\operatorname{cosh}(\omega t)\textbf{i}+r\;\operatorname{sinh}(\omega t)\textbf{j}.$ Find the velocity and acceleration vectors and show that the acceleration is proportional to $\textbf{r}(t).$

answer.solution: With $\mathbf{r}(t)=r\cosh(\omega t)\,\mathbf{i}+r\sinh(\omega t)\,\mathbf{j},$ the velocity is $\mathbf{v}(t)=\mathbf{r}\'(t)=r\omega\sinh(\omega t)\,\mathbf{i}+r\omega\cosh(\omega t)\,\mathbf{j}$ and the acceleration is $\mathbf{a}(t)=\mathbf{v}\'(t)=r\omega^{2}\cosh(\omega t)\,\mathbf{i}+r\omega^{2}\sinh(\omega t)\,\mathbf{j}=\omega^{2}\,\mathbf{r}(t).$ The acceleration is the constant $\omega^{2}$ times the position, so it is proportional to $\mathbf{r}(t),$ and it points directly away from the origin.

answer.solution: $\textbf{v}(t)=(\omega -\omega \;\cos (\omega t))\;\textbf{i}+(\omega \;\sin (\omega t))\;\textbf{j},$ $\textbf{a}(t)=({\omega}^{2}\sin (\omega t))\;\textbf{i}+({\omega}^{2}\cos (\omega t))\;\textbf{j},$ $\text{speed}=\sqrt{{\omega}^{2}-2{\omega}^{2}\cos (\omega t)+{\omega}^{2}{\cos }^{2}(\omega t)+{\omega}^{2}{\sin }^{2}(\omega t)}\;\text{=}\;\sqrt{2{\omega}^{2}(1-\cos (\omega t))}$

A projectile is fired at a height of 1.5 m above the ground with an initial velocity of 100 m/sec and at an angle of 30° above the horizontal. Use this information to answer the following questions:

Prove that an object moving in a straight line at a constant speed has an acceleration of zero.

answer.solution: An object moving in a straight line at a constant speed $c$ has position $\mathbf{r}(t)=\mathbf{r}_{0}+ct\,\mathbf{u},$ where $\mathbf{r}_{0}$ is a point of the line and $\mathbf{u}$ a fixed unit vector along it. Then $\mathbf{v}(t)=\mathbf{r}\'(t)=c\,\mathbf{u},$ a constant vector, of magnitude $c,$ the speed. Differentiating once more, $\mathbf{a}(t)=\mathbf{v}\'(t)=\mathbf{0},$ because the derivative of each component of a constant vector is zero. In terms of components, $a_{\mathbf{T}}=\frac{dv}{dt}=0$ since the speed is constant, and $a_{\mathbf{N}}=\kappa v^{2}=0$ since a line has curvature $\kappa=0.$

Using Kepler’s laws, it can be shown that $v_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r_{0}}}$ is the minimum speed needed when $\theta =0$ so that an object will escape from the pull of a central force resulting from mass M. Use this result to find the minimum speed when $\theta =0$ for a space capsule to escape from the gravitational pull of Earth if the probe is at an altitude of 300 km above Earth’s surface.

Suppose that the position function for an object in three dimensions is given by the equation $\textbf{r}(t)=t\;\cos (t)\textbf{i}+t\;\sin (t)\textbf{j}+3t\;\textbf{k}.$

Show that the particle moves on a circular cone.

answer.solution: With $x=t\cos t,$ $y=t\sin t$ and $z=3t,$ we have $x^{2}+y^{2}=t^{2}(\cos^{2}t+\sin^{2}t)=t^{2},$ so $\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}=|t|$ and $z^{2}=9t^{2}=9(x^{2}+y^{2}).$ Every point of the path satisfies $z^{2}=9(x^{2}+y^{2}),$ the equation of a circular cone with its vertex at the origin and the $z$-axis as its axis: each horizontal cross-section $z=c$ is the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=\frac{c^{2}}{9}.$ For $t\ge 0$ the particle climbs the upper nappe $z=3\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}},$ circling the axis as it rises.

Find the velocity, acceleration, and speed functions. What are the position, velocity, speed, and acceleration of the particle at 1 sec?

answer.solution: $\textbf{v}(t)=\langle 2t,\frac{1}{t},\pi \cos (\pi t)\rangle$ m/sec, $\textbf{a}(t)=\langle 2,-\frac{1}{t^{2}},-{\pi}^{2}\sin (\pi t)\rangle {\;\text{m/sec}}^{2},$ $\text{speed}=\sqrt{4t^{2}+\frac{1}{t^{2}}+{{\pi}^{2}\cos }^{2}(\pi t)}$ m/sec; at $t=1,$ $\textbf{r}(1)=\langle 1,0,0\rangle$ m, $\textbf{v}(1)=\langle 2,1,–π\rangle$ m/sec, $\textbf{a}(1)=\langle 2,-1,0\rangle$ m/sec<sup>2</sup>, and $\text{speed}=\sqrt{5+{\pi}^{2}}$ m/sec

footnotes.html: The vertical component found just above is 1406.25 ft, so the maximum height is 1406.25 ft above the cannon, or 1506.25 ft above sea level.
The display ends with $\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{g}\mathbf{j};$ the distance lies along the horizontal, $\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{g}\mathbf{i},$ as the line before it has it.
